title: Why raindrops don't keep speeding up as they fall
group: HOWN — How and Why in Nature
examples: Why doesn't rain hurt when it hits you?

explain.say: A raindrop starts falling high in a cloud. At first gravity makes it speed up, just like a dropped stone.

draw.text: Why raindrops don't keep speeding up as they fall

explain.say: The faster it falls, the harder the air pushes against it. This drag grows quickly as the speed rises.
Soon the drag pushing up equals the drop's weight pulling down. The forces balance, so the drop stops speeding up and falls at a steady top speed, called its terminal speed.
A big raindrop reaches about 9 metres per second, and a drizzle droplet only about 2. Without air, a drop falling from a cloud 2 kilometres up would hit you at about 700 kilometres per hour.

faq.a: Terminal speed, or terminal velocity, is the steady top speed a falling object reaches when air resistance pushing up equals its weight pulling down. After that it stops speeding up.
Big raindrops fall at about 9 metres per second, roughly 32 kilometres per hour. Small drizzle drops fall at only about 2 metres per second, which is why drizzle seems to float.
asks: What speed does rain hit the ground?

faq.q: Why don't raindrops hurt when they hit you?
faq.a: Air resistance limits their speed, and each drop has very little mass. Without air they would hit at hundreds of kilometres per hour, and rain would be dangerous.
asks: What would rain be like without air?

faq.q: Why do big drops fall faster than small ones?
faq.a: A big drop has much more weight compared with its surface than a small one. It has to fall faster before the air's push can balance its weight, so its terminal speed is higher.
No. Small drops are round, and larger falling drops are flattened by the air underneath into a shape like a burger bun. Very big drops break apart into smaller ones.

facts: Large raindrops about 5 millimetres across fall at roughly 9 metres per second.
Raindrops larger than about 6 millimetres across usually break apart as they fall.

quiz.say: Why does a falling raindrop stop speeding up?
quiz.show: A falling raindrop stops speeding up because…

options.show: Air resistance grows until it equals the drop's weight
options.say: Air resistance grows until it equals the drop's weight

quiz.why: When the upward drag matches the downward weight, the forces balance and the drop falls at a steady terminal speed.

wrong.0: Gravity keeps pulling the whole way down.
wrong.1: The drop's weight stays about the same; it is the drag that grows.
